projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joe H. Petty was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: This is Tuesday August 20, 2002. We are in Terre Haute, Indiana and at the Marine Corps League Office. This is Lane Ralph with Senator Luger's staff. And today I'm interviewing Joe Petty, who served on the War Manpower Commission in World War II as an industrial worker supplying the military and supporting the war effort. And today Joe, he is going to provide us with some background and his experiences and the kind of things that happened at home to supply the troops that served the country during World War II. Joe, your date of birth also is March 6 of 1915?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: So when World War II broke out you were 25 years old?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, I think it's important to start back prior to that time in the Depression years to show what change the civilians went through. There was a period of time there where there weren't any jobs and there was no welfare departments, no food stamps. People were pretty desperate. I had an uncle who committed suicide because he couldn't stand to see his children crying because they didn't get any food.

When I graduated from college at DePaul University I was happy to take a job as a junior interviewer with the state employment service at $1380 a year. When after a year's time, when I got a $5 a month raise to $1440 a year I figured I could get married, but it was one unfortunate twist then. My wife was working, but she was forced to quit when I got married because Indiana didn't want two people from the same family working. They were trying to scatter around, spread around the jobs that were available. The Indiana State Employment Service was setup to get applications, detailed records of unemployed people and contact employers to find job openings and to try to match the qualified workers to the job opening. Then short time later the federal government started the Unemployment Insurance Program which was setup to be handled in our offices which was sort of logical

Remember, many years ago we used to have companies that were in the ice and coal business. They sold ice in the summer in slabs for people to put in their refrigerators and they sold coal in the winter. So really we were the same way. We were always either busy placing people in jobs if things were in good times or helping them draw unemployment insurance if things were in bad shape and they couldn't get new work. We had to sell ourselves to the employers to convince them that our services were free, but they didn't have to use us, so we had to show that we had qualified people that we could make available to their jobs. That sort of changed overnight when we got into the war.

Congress created a new agency called the War Manpower Commission, which was nationwide with the purpose of recruiting and placing qualified people in the jobs that were necessary for the war effort. What made a big change in that when the War Manpower Commission started all of a sudden, a person couldn't take a new job without our permission, and then the employer couldn't hire anybody new without our permission. The War Manpower Commission setup a list for all of the offices of the most essential industries and the most essential occupations and when a person came to us asking us to give them a referral for employment we checked their skill and we could send them to a position that utilized that skill, but not otherwise.

It happened there in Marion that the town, that the highest paying place in town was the brewery, which really wasn't particularly essential to war. And sometimes we had to take people from the brewery and put them in a job at maybe no higher, but a higher skill because they had been machinists but they found out they could get as much money as laborers at the brewery that was easier to do, so we had to get them back into their occupations in a company that was essential to the war effort.

The War Manpower Commission would list them from the highest degree of necessity down to the lowest, and both the companies and the industries. So all of a sudden people couldn't just go out and get a job, they had to come to us and they might find where there's an opening, but they had to come to us and get permission to, a referral to that job in order to be hired. And we had to compare the company and the person's background to our list of essential activity.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Did the companies contact you also when they had a need?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Oh, yes. Uh-huh. They would keep us posted all the time of what their needs were, where they weren't required to do before, but it was to their advantage to do it now because they need these people as quickly as they could get them.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: And they sometimes had quick demands for a certain skill?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah. Unfortunately it was soon after the end of the Depression that the majority of the people didn't have phones in their homes so sometimes when we needed a person right today it was difficult. When each person registered to with us if they didn't have a phone we tried to get them to give us the number of a neighbor, somebody close that would get word to them. And that worked as long as the neighbor was at home, but if the neighbor wasn't at home either, every once in a while I'd sneak out and either walk or drive to the person's home to try to get word to them that they were needed on this job.

But, a day's time now wouldn't make too much difference. But if we could get them on a job a day earlier and the production was picking up a little bit when things were needed for the war. We had plants there that made aircraft parts and parts for tanks, clothing there were plants there. Of course, these companies had perhaps been making things for cars or other civilian things well they were changing over to orders for needs of the military. Same way with the clothing plants, they were making clothing for the people in the military service. And we had several food companies there were in town and they were canning things that were sent to the military in all parts of the world. Of course, we not only had to have them clothed, we had to have them fed from day-to-day. All of a sudden from the stand -- I think that actually a lot of the hundreds of thousands of the early people in the military service had gone on in voluntarily even before Selective Service started because they couldn't find any other jobs. They were already in there but then there got to be a point where the needs were so great that they had to start the Selective Service System, what's called the draft to all people were called, all able-bodied men were called in for interview and physical exam, mental exam, regular routine, so that that brought a lot more men in the service.

And all of a sudden while we've been telling women to stay home so men can get more jobs we are out begging the women to come into the picture. We placed them in some of these places making military implements through training. We had to setup a training program to quickly train people. And people used to talk about Rosie the Riveter and people like that, those were housewives who were put through a crash course on how to do the riveting on aircraft or whatever they were working on.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Did the Manpower Commission help with those training programs?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: How did, what did they do in the training program?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Well, one of the first things that we did, one of our tools was what we called the Dictionary of Occupational Titles, which had been made from, in Washington, which listed oh, thousands and thousands of different occupations. Briefly described the occupations and had a code number for them. When they did the same way with all the job orders from the employers, they'd call for a riveter. We would classify that order with job order with the same code number we were using for the people that have that experience. That was a way for us to get them from the file.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: That's where the standard investigative classification came from?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yes. Then there was another tool that was developed, a system of doing aptitude testing, the general aptitude test battery was developed. And it was a series of written and manual tests that married -- that indicated potential success in several fields of work. So that a lot of these women who had no experiences, some of them too, were put through these tests because it frequently showed that they had potential ability in some line that they'd never even considered before. That was used partly as a beginning step toward getting them into training. There is no use to fit a person in training on something where they would be all thumbs and couldn't handle it, so the test battery showed innate abilities that the people had.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: And for some people that was an eye opener too?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yes, it definitely was. Later on after the war was over we continued to use that in the schools. We went into the high schools and used the test battery with the high school students and gave them the report showing what general fields of work that they showed the greater potential. We didn't tell them they had to go in anything like that but it showed them where they might be more successful. It was an extra tool in their job search. But it was used during the war for, definitely for the jobs created in the war effort.

We had, my wife at that time was working on one part-time clerical job and the editor of the newspaper, The Marion Chronicle, Drysdale Brandon came to our house one day and just begged my wife to come to work as his secretary. So she finally ended up two part-time jobs, she worked for him part-time and in an office part-time. But we had the canning plants there, particularly tomato canning that needed hundreds of women. And they put out pleas everywhere. They finally put out pleas to the churches, wouldn't some of you ladies in the churches come and work. And so my wife and some of the other women from the church decided they would go out to the canning plant and help.

What they did, they peeled tomatoes. And the tomatoes would come down a conveyor line and they had to peel with a knife, they had to peel the tomatoes as they were coming along. And the tomatoes were in water to convey them and the water would splash out on the floors. So most of the time they were standing in water while they peeled. And she sort of laughed because it was done on a piecework basis, you were paid by how many you peeled. And she said always the young girl next to her would peel twice as many as she did because she could peel faster.

But she thought she was helping out however many she got peeled, it helped that much. One time the manager of the plant took some of the women into the laboratory, let them look at some of the material there. They looked at these tomatoes and they saw these little spots on them and asked what they were. And he said those are worm segments, said we need a certain amount of worm segments in the tomatoes to give them flavor. Well, she never learned to eat ketchup after that. I still use it, but she wouldn't eat it because...

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Protein.

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: ...she didn't like those worm segments in there. But he just took it as a matter of fact. Up to that time most of our job placement had just been with companies right in our own area. Our office covered three or four counties around there. But now we went into much heavier, heavier interstate placement. If people were willing to move we'd have the aircraft plant out in Kansas, maybe on the West Coast, that needed their skills and if they would move we could place them in the plants there. And so there was a lot more movement across the country than there had ever been before.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: What, were there national lists that you had of specialized needs?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Uh-huh. And those would be up to date every week so that we'd know changing demands. And we would even post those lists in the office as people were coming in if there was something that they felt that they could handle they would let us know. And we would check their experience, background. And if they were qualified we'd give them the referral out to the plant in that other place. We'd let them know that this individual was coming, give them a little bit of idea what his background was.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Now, A lot of plants had been converted to the war effort, but there were also new plants being built?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Both, that's right, uh-huh. Some of our plants in Terre Haute were converted but in certain other parts of the state as well. All over the country brand new plants were built just specifically for the war needs. So it was a ticklish job from day-to-day of trying to get the workers where they are needed and see that there wasn't a slow down in production just because of lack of qualified workers. And where there weren't enough qualified workers we pushed training more completely to develop people who could step in, maybe as assistants to start, and then learn a little more on the job but they were -- they could much more quickly step into the work. It was a time when I think patriotism was at the top because everybody knew, they all had friends and relatives who were overseas fighting, and they wanted to do whatever they could to help them. So they were willing to get by without a few things they had been accustomed to. We had, by that time we had wage controls, price controls. It wasn't such a thing as a strike or work stoppage or anything like that because people were going to go ahead and work at whatever wages were available and the companies were not going to charge anymore than they had because they were all, they felt they were part of the overall military effort. That went on all during the time with the war and I had, I thought a real strange reaction at the end of the war. The day that it was announced that armistice was here a lot of the people were crying, but it was because they were so relieved. But we discovered that some of the women out in the plants were crying because they knew that would be the end of their jobs. So even though it's a patriotic feeling, they had gotten used to working and they knew now, they were told, they understood all along that they were working for the duration and when men came back they'd get their old jobs back. So then we came a point where all of a sudden women could hardly find jobs again. And it was a few years until it got to the point now where they have equal opportunity in employment and, you know, in all phases.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: And the war also, didn't some of the plants have to have special situations for women where maybe children came to the plant with them?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah, that's true. Yes. They setup little nurseries for the children right at the plant. And they were willing if they were short enough to let the women work part-time, certain hours. If they, maybe they'd put two people on a shift one work four hours, and then another come in. They had -- they made as many adjustments as they could in order to take someone who did have children.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: How about you mentioned earlier the changes on wages and --

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: -- and restrictions on employment and those and no strikes and whatever. What about rationing, did you have rationing?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Oh, yes. Food was rationed, clothing was rationed, and gasoline was rationed. I had a personal situation there where we were rationed, gasoline rationing was mandated. It was just enough to get around in town, just get us to work and back, but not across open country to other cities. I had grown up in Lafayette and my mother was in Lafayette about 75 miles from Marion dying of cancer. And I didn't go to see her because I thought it was too unpatriotic to ask for special allowance of extra gasoline to go over there. I had mixed feelings. I wanted to see her, but I just thought that extra gasoline is being taken away from somebody who might need it in their trip to their tanks or someplace overseas. So I think that people, that is just an example of how people did, they feel they sacrificed a little bit along with the people that were in the military because we were all in the same boat. We were going to sink or swim together.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: You also, didn't you have tires were even rationed, weren't they, rubber products?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah, that's right.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Hard to get a tire.

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: There was a pretty heavy retreading business in that case. It was saving of rubber to put treads on the old tires and keep on using them as long as you could.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: A lot of those businesses cropped up, huh?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah. Well, unless there are other questions I don't know of anything else particularly to mention now.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: What about families, like you mentioned. How did people get around transportation-wise to the factories and what did people do to get to work in those days?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Well, if you had cars, of course, they had to pool, get as many people in the car as possible. In those days we still in Indiana in some sections still have what we called the urban wheel (ph) electric trains a little bigger than the street cars in the city, but they would go from town to town and go from Lafayette to Frankfort and different cities in the surrounding parts of the state. A lot of people got back and forth on those urban wheel (ph) what you call them these days.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Pretty extensive system. I think they went from South Bend to Indianapolis to Louisville and Richmond to Terre Haute.

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yes. And then, of course, there weren't airlines then so the travel, like these people going clear out to the West Coast or the East Coast, that was all by train. Some of the people, occasionally they could move their families with them, but it did split up quite a few families because the wife might stay home with the kids while the husband was going out to a job in another part of the country. But they were willing to do that. Maybe in some cases later on a man might be able to send for his family, but in some cases they were separated as long as a person was on that job away from home.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: And on those trains they not only passengers at that time, they also have a lot of other functions, didn't they?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Well, they always had servicemen going to wherever they would report to. And the civilians would have canteens at the stops where they'd bring in the sandwiches and soft drinks and things like that. So they -- and cigarettes, things of that kind for the servicemen. And it's true that the trains now were separated, but then you might have three or four passenger cars and then fill the freight cars right on the same trains hauling goods, military goods. I still sort of miss the old cabooses that used to be on the end of them. Now there is just an abrupt end to the train, but there used to be a man on the end there who was sort of a flagman and he could communicate with the locomotive engineer. Transportation was difficult. It had to be as much as possible mass transportation to save on fuel. They got them to their jobs and back the most economical way possible.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: But trains you could get around fairly well too?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Connect to other locations?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah, other remote train lines then, and just sort of like the airlines connect now, you could, you might go through several different lines before you got to your destination, but they -- it was hard to get in, they met, they didn't really have to wait, they were tied together so that you could just move from one train into the next until the next stop.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Joe, are there any other comments you want to make about the War Manpower Commission and the experience you had with that during the war and how that affected your life?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Well, I think it made me understand more of human nature and how if we could work together then it's just a shame that then, different countries worked together in a cooperative effort. It's a little shame today that so many countries and individuals can't get along. There seem to be internal squabbles of all kinds. If we could get back to the feeling of teamwork and family that we had during World War II I think maybe we could solve some of our international problems now. Nobody would in those days, would even though we were fighting against, bitterly against an enemy I don't think our schools did the way schools in some parts of the world do now, is training the kids from infancy to hate their enemies. That's a hard thing to combat. I don't know how we are going to get squared around until we reach a point where we can understand again, that we are all part of the human race and we're here together, and we should try to work together instead of at odds all the time. We've read some of these more recent books calling it -- that's a great generation back at that time. And I think it is true, not that people became famous or anything like that, but just in their own quiet ways they were contributing to the country and its welfare.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Rolled up their sleeves and went to work.

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: And worked with purpose then?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Yeah, that's right.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Any other comments you want to make before we conclude?

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Well, only that I do appreciate the opportunity to give you this information. I'm pleased to hear that it will be maintained because I realize how easy it is for a generation to lose track of what prior generations did and this is one way of keeping our heritage alive.

sp.speaker: Lane Ralph
sp.p: Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Joe H. Petty
sp.p: Okay.
[Conclusion of interview]
